items.title: Give every quantity a job
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: When a maths problem gives you three numbers, each number can do a different job. One might count packets. Another might tell you how many counters fit in each packet. The third might count counters on their own. Give every number its job before you calculate. Start with the question: how many counters altogether? That tells us the unit of our answer. Four plus three plus two gives nine, but we would be adding a packet count to two different descriptions of counters. Give each quantity its label and ask what it would take to get everything into counters. Mia has four packets of counters. Each packet contains three counters, and Mia has two loose counters as well. How many counters does she have altogether? Before you work it out, point to what the four, the three and the two each describe. Four tells us how many groups there are. Three tells us the size of every group. Open the first packet and you can see three counters. Open the others and the same group repeats. Four groups of three give twelve counters. Multiplication gives the counter total for the packets. The two loose counters are already in the unit we want. Slide them into the collection. Now we are adding twelve counters and two counters, and the total is fourteen counters. Check it in the picture: four rows of three, and two beside them. The same idea works with measurements. One ribbon is two metres long, and another is thirty centimetres long. How much ribbon is there altogether? Two metres is two hundred centimetres. Both lengths are now in centimetres, so together they measure two hundred and thirty centimetres. A number can have a different job even when it uses the same digits. Think of a book with pages numbered ninety-five through one hundred and five. In just that range, how many times is the digit nine written? Look across the page numbers and find each printed nine. Five page numbers contain a nine: ninety-five, ninety-six, ninety-seven, ninety-eight and ninety-nine. The last page number on that list contains two nines. Its first nine counts once and its second nine counts once. There are six written nines in all. Read the final question. Label each number with what it counts or measures. Bring quantities into a common unit when you need to add them. Here is your notebook challenge. Six boxes hold eight pencils each. Five pencils are broken. How many unbroken pencils are there? Label the quantities and show your calculation.

items.title: Choose a representation that exposes the relationship
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: A difficult-looking question can become much clearer as soon as you draw the right picture. A line shows order. A table sets comparisons side by side. A sketch makes shapes and boundaries visible. An equation holds a relationship in place. Choose the one that helps you see what the question is asking. Picture a fence. Your eye can follow every post or every panel between two posts. A sketch gives both counts a place on the same line. The words each end tell us where the fence starts and stops. Mark those ends first. Then look for what repeats between them. A straight fence is thirty metres long. There is a post at each end, and the posts are five metres apart. How many posts are there? Draw the full thirty metres. Mark the left end as zero, and mark off spaces of five metres. Thirty metres divided into five-metre spaces gives six gaps. Follow each gap to its right-hand end. That accounts for six posts. The post at zero sits before the first gap, so add it once. Six gaps, plus that starting post, makes seven posts. Now join the ends to make a closed fence, using the same six equal panels. Watch the last post come back to the very first one. They meet at a single corner. Each panel now ends at a different post, and all posts are included. That makes six gaps and six posts. Try the same kind of line with a queue. Sam is ninth from the front and sixth from the back. How many people are there? Eight stand in front of Sam, and five stand behind. Eight, plus Sam, plus five, makes fourteen. Both ranks include Sam, so give Sam one place in the picture. A table helps when there are several things to compare. Box A contains eight pencils and costs sixteen dollars. Box B contains four pencils and costs twelve dollars. Add a price per pencil column. The divisions give two dollars and three dollars. Box A costs more for the box and less for each pencil. A sketch reveals a boundary. Join two mats, each four metres by three metres, along their three-metre sides. How much edge is exposed? Each mat has fourteen metres around it. The pair has twenty-eight before joining. The shared edge removes three metres from each mat, so the equation gives twenty-two metres outside. Choose a line for order and gaps, a table for comparisons, and a sketch for shape and boundaries. Use an equation to show how the quantities fit together. Your turn. Trees are planted every four metres along a forty-metre path, including both ends. How many trees are there? Sketch it first.

items.title: Use the model to check the answer
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: Imagine a calculation gives seven and a half people in a queue. A headcount has to be a whole number. That tells you to look back at your reasoning. Start problems by asking what a sensible answer could look like. Then use that idea to check the result. A count of buses is a whole number. A probability is between zero and one, including both ends. An area has square units. Three metres along each side of a square gives nine square metres. Identify the kind of answer first. The model also helps you predict its size. One hundred and thirty students are going on a trip. Each bus has seats for forty students. What is the smallest number of buses that can take the whole group? Make a quick estimate before you continue. Think about what happens if a bus is only partly full. Group the students into forties. One bus takes forty. A second takes another forty. A third brings the total on board to one hundred and twenty. There are still ten students waiting. Write one hundred and thirty as three lots of forty plus ten. Those ten students still need seats. Put them in a fourth bus. Ten of its forty seats are used, so thirty are spare. Everyone now has a seat, and the answer is four buses. Check both sides of the boundary. Four buses make one hundred and sixty seats, enough for all one hundred and thirty students. Three buses make one hundred and twenty seats, so ten students would be left out. Any smaller number has even fewer seats. Four is the smallest number that works. Keep the same trip. This time ask how many buses are completely full if the driver fills each bus before opening the next. Each of the first three has forty students. The fourth has ten. So three buses are full. The last sentence of the question tells you which count to give. Predict what a sensible answer should look like. Check every condition, then reread the question. Here is your notebook challenge. Pack one hundred eggs into boxes of twelve. Fill each box before opening the next. How many boxes are needed, and how many eggs go in the last box?

items.title: Read the question into a useful model
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: A ribbon lies along a centimetre ruler. Its left edge lines up with two, and its right edge lines up with nine. How long is the ribbon? Look at where it begins and ends, then try to explain your first move. The mark labelled two is two centimetres from zero. The mark labelled nine is nine centimetres from zero. The question asks for the distance from the first position to the second. Trace that part of the ruler with your finger. Move from two to three. That is the first centimetre. From three to four is the second. Every small step adds one centimetre. Keep going until you reach nine. There are seven gaps of one centimetre, so the ribbon is seven centimetres long. The nine centimetres from zero to the end includes two centimetres before the ribbon begins. Remove those two centimetres. Nine minus two leaves seven. You can count eight marked points across the ribbon because both ends have a mark. Each centimetre lives in the space between two marks. Slide the ribbon two centimetres to the left. Watch both ends move the same distance. It starts at zero and reaches seven. The two endpoints changed together, and the span stayed seven centimetres. That is another way to check our answer. The same idea works with time. A film starts at seven fifteen in the evening and ends at nine oh five. How many minutes pass? Draw a timeline. Put seven fifteen on the left. Mark eight o'clock and nine o'clock along the way, and stop at nine oh five. From seven fifteen to eight o'clock is forty-five minutes. The next hour gives sixty minutes. From nine o'clock to the end is five more. Add forty-five, sixty and five. The total is one hundred and ten minutes. That is one hour and fifty minutes. Label the two positions. Find the length, or the time, between them. Use equal steps and check the units. Now try your own timeline. A camera starts filming at ten forty-seven in the morning and stops at twelve oh six that day. How many minutes does it record?

items.title: Find an invariant by inspecting one move
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Here's a puzzle. One pile has five gold counters. The other has seven blue counters. You may move counters between the piles, as often as you like. Could you finish with ten counters in each pile? Before you try dozens of moves, ask a better question. Is there something that no legal move can change? Watch closely. Move two blue counters to the gold pile. Now there are seven on the left and five on the right. The picture has changed, but the total is still twelve. Every transfer takes some counters away from one pile and adds exactly that many to the other. Nothing is created. Nothing disappears. So ten and ten is impossible. That would require twenty counters, and we have only twelve. Six and six, however, is possible. A quantity that remains unchanged after every permitted move is called an invariant. Here, the invariant is the total number of counters. But here's the twist. Change the rule. Each move now adds two brand-new counters to both piles. What stays fixed this time? The total is growing, by four with every move. So the total is no longer an invariant. Look at the difference between the two piles instead. We begin with five and seven: a gap of two. Add two to each and we get seven and nine. Add two again, and we get nine and eleven. The gap is always two. Let's prove this, rather than just spot a pattern. Call the two pile sizes A and B. After a move, their sizes are A plus two and B plus two. Now subtract the new sizes. The positive two and negative two cancel perfectly. We are left with A minus B. So the difference cannot change. Go back to transferring counters. If the first pile loses t and the second gains t, the total becomes A minus t, plus B plus t. Again, the changes cancel. Here's the important trap. Moving counters preserves the total, but not usually the difference. Adding the same number to both preserves their difference, but changes the total. Try one yourself. Start with four counters in one pile and nine in the other. Each move adds two counters to both. Could you reach eighteen and twenty-three? Yes. The difference starts at five and ends at five. Exactly seven moves add fourteen counters to each pile. Both target numbers work. But could you reach eighteen and twenty-two? No. Their difference is four, not five. The invariant rules that out instantly. This is the power of an invariant. You don't need to simulate a hundred moves. Examine one move, identify what cancels, and use that to reason about every move. Pause here. Draw one move in your notebook, and write a single equation showing what remains unchanged.
items.extended_reading: This section is called Find an invariant by inspecting one move. An invariant is a quantity that does not change when a permitted move is made. It might be a total, a difference, a product, a remainder or a colour balance. Start by comparing the state immediately before and immediately after one move. A claim about a long process becomes much easier to justify if every individual move preserves the same quantity. SEE IT Two moves, two different invariants A transfer moves existing units between piles, so their total stays fixed. Adding two new units to each pile preserves the difference instead. A transfer between two piles preserves their combined total. If t is transferred from the first pile to the second, the signed difference “first minus second” decreases by 2t. To find the absolute gap, also check whether the piles exchange order. By contrast, adding the same amount to both piles preserves their difference but changes their total. Naming the operation prevents these two situations from being confused. A038 and A112 are useful places to look for a preserved difference rather than solve several unrelated unknowns. If objects come in two types with different per-object contributions, compare the real collection with a starting model made entirely from one type. Keep the object count fixed. Each replacement changes the total by the same difference, so the total change determines how many replacements occurred. Check both the object count and the final total. A014 and A056 fit this comparison method. Sometimes the visible entries are not the quantities worth tracking. Try a small adjustment such as adding or subtracting a fixed amount from each entry. Expand the rule and look for cancellation or factorisation. N1.26 invites this kind of search. The important proof has two parts: identify a candidate quantity, then show algebraically that one legal move leaves it unchanged. A pattern noticed in a few trials is only a clue. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

items.title: Work backwards: undo the last move first
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Sometimes a maths puzzle tells you the finish, but hides the start. Working backwards means beginning with that finish and undoing the moves. There is one crucial rule: undo the last move first. Like taking off your shoes before your socks, the order matters. This is useful when guessing the starting number would take ages. If each move can be undone, we can follow a clear route back to the start. Then we check the answer by travelling forwards again. Let's try a number machine. It multiplies a secret number by four, then adds three. The machine finishes at twenty-three. What number went in? Notice the order: multiply first, then add. Start at twenty-three. The last thing the machine did was add three, so undo that first. Twenty-three minus three is twenty. We have recovered the amount just before the final addition. Only now do we undo the multiplication. Twenty divided by four is five. Check the whole journey: five times four is twenty, and twenty plus three is twenty-three. Five works. What if we undo the operations in the wrong order? Twenty-three divided by four is five point seven five. Subtract three, and we get two point seven five. That is not five. The order is part of the method. Here is why the correct order works for any starting number. Call the start x. The machine makes four x plus three. Subtracting three leaves four x. Dividing by four leaves x. We peel away the outside operation first. Multiplying by zero would lose the starting information, so that move cannot be undone uniquely. Now try a different kind of puzzle. A child keeps half of a collection of counters. Then they keep two thirds of what remains. At the end, there are eight counters. How many were there at the start? Work backwards from eight. These eight counters are two thirds of the previous pile. Split them into two equal groups of four. Restore the missing third, another group of four. The previous pile had twelve counters. Twelve was half of the original collection. Double it to recover twenty-four. Now check forwards. Half of twenty-four is twelve. Two thirds of twelve is eight. Every stage agrees. The common trap is using the wrong whole. Two thirds of what remains means two thirds of twelve, not two thirds of the original twenty-four. Write the amount after every stage so the whole stays clear. There is one more check when a puzzle uses whole counters. Every intermediate pile must also be whole. Suppose a rule halves the pile, adds one counter, then doubles it. Could the final pile contain seven? Undo the steps. Seven divided by two is three point five. Subtract one to get two point five. Double it to get five. The starting number is whole, but the intermediate piles are not. You cannot have half a counter in this puzzle. So seven is impossible under these rules. Try eight instead. Backwards, eight becomes four, then three, then six. Forwards, six becomes three, then four, then eight. Every pile is whole, and every move is legal. Remember the method. Reverse the order. Undo each operation. Check every intermediate state. Then check the complete forward journey. A backward calculation finds a candidate; the checks show whether it really works. Your turn. A number is multiplied by three, then four is subtracted. The result is seventeen. Pause here. Recover the starting number, then draw the forward journey to prove your answer.

items.title: Compare different orders of the same operations
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Start with three. Add two and then double. Five becomes ten. Try the same start with the operations swapped. Double three first, then add two. Six becomes eight. The same steps can give different results when their order changes. Testing more starting numbers might help us guess a pattern. A letter lets us explain the pattern for every starting number. We'll compare the two operation orders side by side and look for the part that changes. Choose any starting number. Order A adds five and then doubles. Order B doubles and then adds five. Which order gives the bigger result, and by how much? Try one starting number before we compare them all. Call the starting number x. In Order A, adding five makes a bar with an x part and a five part. Doubling makes two copies of that whole bar. Collect its parts. Two copies of x and two fives give two x plus ten. Order B doubles x first. That gives two copies of x. Add five once. Both orders now show two copies of the starting value and at least one five. Pair those matching pieces. The extra five in Order A is the entire difference. What if we multiply by negative two instead? In Order A, the five is multiplied too, so its contribution is negative ten. Order B still adds positive five. The common part is negative two x in both orders. Positive five is fifteen more than negative ten, so Order B now wins by fifteen. Two additions can swap because we still add the same total. Two multiplications can swap because their combined scale is the same. When you mix the two types of step, look closely at whether an amount added later gets scaled at all. Give the start a letter. Write the two orders separately. Compare the parts that match and calculate the difference. In your notebook, compare subtracting four and then multiplying by three with multiplying by three and then subtracting four. Which gives the greater result, and by how much?

items.title: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Start with any whole number, including zero. Rule A adds three and then multiplies by four. Rule B multiplies by four and then adds three. Which output is larger, and by how much? Sketch one example before looking for a proof. Call the start x. Rule A forms x plus three and makes four copies of the whole amount. Look at one copy. It contains an x tile and a three tile. Four copies give four x tiles and four threes, so the result is four x plus twelve. In Rule B, the multiplication acts on the starting value. Make four copies of x. Now add the three. This time the three comes in once, after the copying step. The result is four x plus three. Line up the outputs. Each side contains four copies of the same x and one added three. Pair those tiles. There are three extra threes in Rule A. Their total is nine. Whatever whole number we pick at the start, Rule A is larger by nine. Check the smallest allowed input. Starting from zero gives twelve and three. Starting from ten gives fifty-two and forty-three. Each difference is nine. In both rows, the starting amount changes the two outputs by the same amount. The multiplication makes extra copies of the added amount when the addition comes first. Use that observation with two new rules. One adds two before multiplying by six. The other multiplies by six before adding two. Draw the matching pieces and find the gap.

items.title: Read a remainder as a precise statement
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Seventeen counters make three full groups of five, with two left over. That leftover is called the remainder. The three full groups give a multiple of five. The two counters tell you exactly how far seventeen is past that multiple. When we divide whole numbers by five, the possible remainders are zero, one, two, three and four. A leftover of five would make another complete group. However large the starting number, it fits into one of these five remainder classes. A necklace repeats red, blue, green and yellow in that order. The first bead is red. What colour is bead fifty? Try marking the boundaries between the repeating groups of four. A full cycle has four beads. Fifty is twelve groups of four, plus two more beads. The twelve groups take us to bead forty-eight. Count two beads into the next cycle. Its second colour is blue, so bead fifty is blue. Bead forty-eight lands on a complete group boundary. It has remainder zero when divided by four. In this position list we count from one, so a complete group finishes on its fourth bead. Bead forty-eight is yellow. Twenty-three is four groups of five plus three. Thirty-eight is seven groups of five plus three. In the difference, the two leftovers cancel. Three extra groups of five give fifteen. And adding any whole group of five leaves a remainder unchanged. That is why equal remainders and a multiple-of-five difference go together. Try combining two conditions. Below thirty, the numbers with remainder three on division by five are three, eight, thirteen, eighteen, twenty-three and twenty-eight. Now test them for remainder one on division by three. Only thirteen and twenty-eight reach that column. A remainder tells how far you are past a multiple. It must be smaller than the divisor. For a repeating pattern, decide which position sits at remainder zero. Here is your notebook challenge. Today is Tuesday. What day will it be one hundred days from now?

items.title: Separate the first coincidence from the repeat period
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Two lights repeat at different speeds. One flashes every four seconds and the other every six. We can ask when they first flash together after starting. We can also ask how much time separates one meeting from the next. Twenty-four is a multiple of both four and six. A smaller common multiple may also work. First mark where each light starts. Then add its own period each time. A timeline shows both the starting positions and the repeated jumps. Both lights flash at time zero. One repeats every four seconds. The other repeats every six seconds. When do they next flash together? List a few times for each light, and line up the lists. The first light flashes at four, eight, twelve and sixteen. The second flashes at six, twelve and eighteen. Their first positive meeting is at twelve seconds. Twelve is the lowest common multiple of four and six. A gap between meetings has to be a multiple of both periods, so the next meeting is twelve seconds later. Let the second light start at time two. Its times are two, eight, fourteen and twenty. The first light's times stay on the multiples of four. The first meeting moves to eight seconds, and the next is at twenty. The starting offset changed the first meeting. The twelve-second gap stayed the same. Now start the second light at time one. Its jumps of six keep all its times odd. Starting from zero and moving in jumps of four keeps the other times even. An odd time and an even time cannot match, so these two lights never flash together. When meetings are possible, the lowest common multiple gives the gap between them. The starting positions decide when the first meeting happens. In your notebook, one bus leaves every eight minutes and another every twelve. They both leave at nine o'clock. When do they next leave together?

items.title: Build guarantees with the pigeonhole principle
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Put four counters into three boxes. You can place the first three with one in each box. The fourth has to join a counter somewhere. If you already put two together earlier, the claim already holds. This is the pigeonhole principle. A guarantee asks what must happen in every possible case. Imagine the arrangement that delays the result for as long as possible. Its limit helps us find the smallest count that will force the result. The important decision is what the boxes represent. A drawer contains many socks of exactly four colours. You take socks without looking. What is the smallest number you must take to guarantee two of the same colour? Try to plan a draw that delays the first matching pair. Use one box for each colour. Begin with one sock in each box. That is a possible draw of four socks with no match. The fifth sock has to go into one of the occupied boxes. Five is sufficient, and this example with four proves that five is the minimum. The boxes can stand for remainders. Take any four different whole numbers. When we divide by three, the possibilities are zero, one and two. Two of the four numbers share a remainder. Take their difference. The leftover parts cancel, leaving a multiple of three. Choose six different numbers from one to ten. Group the ten numbers into five pairs that add to eleven. A choice of six puts two numbers in one of those five pair boxes. Both members of that pair have been chosen, and they add to eleven. Choose the objects and choose the boxes. Compare their counts. When the problem asks for the smallest guarantee, show how one fewer could fail. In your notebook, how many people must be in a room to guarantee two birthdays in the same month?

items.title: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Choose any four different whole numbers. Prove that two of them always have a difference that is a multiple of three. You can choose very large numbers if you like. How can one argument cover every possible choice? Divide a whole number by three. The remainder can be zero, one or two. A leftover of three would make another complete group. Create one box for each of the three allowable remainders. Every chosen number belongs to exactly one box. Four numbers and three boxes force at least two numbers into the same box. Those two numbers have the same remainder. We can use that single fact to show their difference is a multiple of three. Write the larger number as three a plus r, and the smaller as three b plus the same r. On subtracting, the two r terms cancel. The result is three times the difference between a and b. It is a whole number of groups of three. Try two, six, ten and thirteen. Ten and thirteen both leave remainder one. Their difference is three. Could three numbers guarantee the result? With one, two and three, the remainders all differ. Their differences are one or two. This shows four is the smallest number that guarantees a match. Choose a box for each remainder and use subtraction once two numbers share a box. Now increase the divisor to ten. How many different whole numbers guarantee that two differ by a multiple of ten? Show both why your answer works and how one fewer choice could fail.

items.title: Factor with a purpose
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: Whole numbers bigger than one are made by multiplying primes. A prime has exactly two positive factors, one and itself. Take sixty. Split it into six and ten, then split those again. The prime pieces are two, three, two and five. Start another way. Write sixty as four times fifteen. Four gives two twos, and fifteen gives a three and a five. Rearrange the pieces in increasing order and both trees give the same list. That fixed prime factorisation is why we can work with the pieces. Is ninety-one prime? Decide which small primes you would try first, and think about how far the search needs to go. Ninety-one is odd, so two fails. Its digits add to ten, so three fails. Its last digit is one, so five fails. Try seven. Seven times thirteen equals ninety-one. These two factors show that ninety-one is composite. If both factors were bigger than the square root, multiplying them would give too much. So a composite number has a prime factor at or below its square root. For ninety-seven that root lies between nine and ten. Try two, three, five and seven. All leave a remainder, so ninety-seven is prime. Three different whole numbers, each bigger than one, multiply to sixty-six. Which numbers are they? Sixty-six has exactly three prime pieces, two, three and eleven. Each of the three numbers needs a piece. Each gets exactly one, so those three primes are the answer. Split a number until all its pieces are prime. When you test whether a number is prime, use the small primes up to its square root. One has only one positive factor. In your notebook, write eighty-four as a product of primes.

items.title: Count divisors by making independent choices
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: Twelve has six positive factors: one, two, three, four, six and twelve. We can list those by finding the products that make twelve. For a larger number, it is easier to count choices from its prime factorisation. Three hundred and sixty factorises into two cubed, three squared and five. Its full factor list has twenty-four entries. We can account for them through three small counts, one for each prime. Let's see how this works with twelve first. Twelve is two times two times three. A factor of twelve is made from some of those prime tiles. Think about how many twos you can use. Then think about your choices for the three. How many different products are possible? Use zero, one or two twos. That gives three choices. For each of them, either include the three or leave it out. That gives two choices. Three times two makes six products. Taking no tiles gives one. Taking all the tiles gives twelve. Every cell makes a different factor. Seventy-two is two cubed times three squared. Choose zero, one, two or three twos. For each choice there are three possibilities for the threes. Four times three gives twelve factors. For three hundred and sixty, the extra choice about the five doubles that count to twenty-four. For thirty-six, the factor pairs are one and thirty-six, two and eighteen, three and twelve, and four and nine. Six pairs with itself, so it appears just once in the list. A factor pairs with itself exactly when its square is the number. That is why square numbers have an odd count of positive factors. For each prime, include the choice to use zero copies. Add one to the prime's exponent, and multiply the resulting counts. In your notebook, find the number of positive factors of two hundred, then explain why your method counts each factor once.

items.title: Track prime copies through several conditions
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: Write twelve as two times two times three. Write eighteen as two times three times three. Group copies of the same prime vertically. One column holds the twos. Another holds the threes. We can see exactly how many of each prime each number uses. We can solve three problems using these counts. To divide into both numbers, a factor needs to fit inside both rows. A common multiple has to contain both rows. For a square, the tiles must split into two matching sets. Find the largest positive number that divides both twelve and eighteen. Then find the smallest positive number that is a multiple of both. Use the tiles, and decide how many copies of each prime you need. A common factor can use only the copies both numbers can supply. Eighteen can supply one two and twelve can supply one three. Those are the smaller counts in the two columns. The highest common factor is two times three, which is six. A common multiple needs enough copies to cover either number. Twelve needs two twos. Eighteen needs two threes. Take the larger count in each column. Two twos and two threes multiply to thirty-six. It is the lowest common multiple. For each prime, the smaller count plus the larger count equals the original two counts added together. So the factors of six and thirty-six together use exactly the same prime copies as twelve and eighteen together. Both products are two hundred and sixteen. A square needs two matching groups of prime tiles. Thirty-six splits into two sixes. Forty-eight has four twos and one three. The three has no partner. Multiply by another three and the tiles can split evenly. The new total is one hundred and forty-four, or twelve squared. Use the smaller prime counts for a highest common factor. Use the larger counts for a lowest common multiple. A square has even counts of every prime. In your notebook, find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple of twenty and thirty.

items.title: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: What is the smallest positive whole number that you can multiply ninety by to make a perfect square? Try to think of ninety as a collection of prime pieces. A square will let those pieces split into two identical groups. Ninety factorises into two times three times three times five. Each prime needs an even number of copies in a square. The threes already make a pair. The two and the five each appear once. Put a space for a partner beside each of them. Supply one more two and one more five. Those are the missing tiles. Their product is ten, so multiplying ninety by ten adds just the two partners we need. Now each prime has an even count. Ninety times ten is nine hundred. Split its tiles into two identical groups, each with a two, a three and a five. Each group multiplies to thirty. Thirty times thirty is nine hundred, so the new number is a square. Could a smaller positive multiplier work? Any multiplier that works must supply a two and a five, because those counts start odd. A number divisible by the two distinct primes two and five is a multiple of ten. Ten is the first positive multiple and we have shown it works. For a square, pair every prime. Choose one partner for each prime whose count is odd. Try the same proof with sixty. Find the smallest positive whole number to multiply sixty by to make a square, and check your answer by splitting the new prime tiles into two equal groups.

items.title: Decide whether order belongs to the outcome
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: Before counting anything, ask one question: does order matter? Choosing a winner and a runner-up is different from choosing a team of two. On the podium, swapping the two people changes the result. In a team, swapping them changes nothing. Getting this wrong doubles your answer, or halves it. It is one of the most common counting mistakes, and the cure is to decide about order before you start multiplying. Three runners, Ava, Ben and Cal, are in a race. In how many ways can first and second place be filled? And how many different pairs of them could form a team? Pause and try both. For the podium, there are three choices for first place, then two remaining choices for second. Three times two is six ordered results. For a team, Ava then Ben is the same team as Ben then Ava. The six ordered results merge in pairs, leaving three teams. We divide by two because each team was counted in two orders. Now choose three people from five. In order, that is five times four times three, which is sixty. As an unordered group, each set of three people can be arranged in six orders, so sixty divided by six gives ten groups. The number you divide by is the number of ways to arrange the chosen objects. Read the wording carefully. If the three chosen people get different jobs, such as captain, scorer and timekeeper, then order matters again and the answer is sixty. If positions or roles differ, count in order. If only membership matters, divide by the number of arrangements of the chosen group. Notebook challenge: from six players, how many ways are there to choose a captain and a vice-captain? And how many ways to choose two players to carry the equipment?

items.title: Split by the restriction that changes the choices
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: Some counting problems are too awkward to do in one go. The trick is to split them into cases. Good cases have two properties: no outcome belongs to two cases, and every outcome belongs to one. Multiplying choices only works when the number of choices does not depend on what you chose earlier. When a restriction changes the choices, a single multiplication breaks. Splitting at the restriction repairs it. Using the digits zero, one, two, three and four, with no digit repeated, how many even three-digit numbers can be made? Pause and think about which place causes the trouble. The number must be even, so the last digit is zero, two or four. But zero is special, because a number cannot start with zero. So split by the last digit: either it is zero, or it is two or four. If the last digit is zero, the first digit has four choices and the middle has three: twelve numbers. If the last digit is two or four, the first digit cannot be zero or the last digit, leaving three choices, and the middle has three. That is two times three times three: eighteen numbers. The cases cannot overlap, because a number has only one last digit. Add them: twelve plus eighteen is thirty. Sometimes it is quicker to count what is forbidden. Two switches have four settings altogether. If "both on" is not allowed, subtract that one, leaving three. Counting everything and subtracting the unwanted part is called using the complement. Split at the feature that changes the choices. Multiply within a case. Add the cases. Notebook challenge: how many two-digit numbers have two different digits?

items.title: Prove that the classification is reversible
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: A counting method is correct when every outcome has exactly one address. From the outcome you can tell which choices made it, and every set of choices makes a real outcome. If both are true, nothing is missed and nothing is counted twice. Double counting and missed cases are invisible if you only look at the final number. Checking the addresses is the way to trust a count without redoing it. Five different students sit in a row of five seats. Three are girls and two are boys. The two boys must not sit next to each other. In how many ways can they be seated? Pause and look for a way to build every legal row exactly once. Seat the girls first. Three girls can be arranged in six orders. Around them are four gaps: one at each end and two between. Put each boy into a different gap. The first boy has four gaps to choose from, and the second has three. That is twelve ways, so there are six times twelve, seventy-two seatings. Now check the addresses. Take any legal row. Remove the boys and you see the girls' order. Look where the boys were and you see which gaps they used. So each legal row comes from exactly one set of choices. The count is complete and has no repeats. A second method confirms it. Five people can sit in one hundred and twenty ways. Glue the boys together as one block: four objects in twenty-four orders, times two for the boys swapping. That is forty-eight unwanted rows. One hundred and twenty minus forty-eight is seventy-two. Ask two questions of any counting method. Can I recover the choices from every legal outcome? And does every choice give a legal outcome? Notebook challenge: in how many ways can four different books stand on a shelf if two particular books must not be next to each other?

items.title: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: A lunch has one sandwich, cheese or bean, and one fruit, apple, pear or plum. Cheese may not be paired with plum. How many different lunches are possible? The restriction only mentions cheese, so split by sandwich. A lunch has exactly one sandwich, so these two cases cannot overlap. With cheese, plum is not allowed, so the allowed fruits are apple and pear. That is two lunches: cheese with apple, and cheese with pear. With bean, all three fruits are allowed. That is three lunches. Add the cases: two plus three is five. Check another way. Without the rule there would be two times three, six lunches. Exactly one of them, cheese with plum, is forbidden. Six minus one is five. Two methods agree. When branches have different sizes, add them rather than multiplying. Rebuild the tree yourself, then try this: there are three shirts and four pairs of shorts, but the red shirt cannot be worn with the two orange pairs. How many outfits are possible?

items.title: Count incidences before counting objects
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: Every handshake has two hands in it. That small fact is surprisingly powerful. If each person reports how many hands they shook, and you add up the reports, every handshake has been counted twice, once by each person. Counting something in two different ways gives you an equation for free. It lets you count lines by counting ends, or faces by counting edges, without drawing the whole picture. Six people meet, and everyone shakes hands once with everyone else. How many handshakes take place? Pause and think about what each person would report. Each person shakes hands with the five others, so each person reports five. Six reports of five add to thirty. But each handshake was reported by both of the people in it. So thirty counts every handshake twice. Thirty divided by two is fifteen handshakes. The same idea can prove something is impossible. Can seven people each shake hands with exactly three others? The reports would add to twenty-one. But the total of the reports is always twice the number of handshakes, so it must be even. Twenty-one is odd. It cannot be done. It works for solids too. A cube has six faces, and each face has four edges: twenty-four reports. Every edge belongs to two faces, so there are twelve edges. Let each object report what it touches. Add the reports. Then divide by how many times each item was reported. Notebook challenge: in a tournament, eight teams each play every other team once. How many games are played?

items.title: Give each component its contribution
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: Sometimes you cannot measure things one at a time. You only know totals of pairs. The useful trick is to add all the measurements and ask how many times each unknown has been counted. This replaces trial and error with one clean step. Instead of guessing the three values, you find their total first, and everything else follows by subtraction. Three boxes are weighed in pairs. The first and second weigh ten kilograms together. The second and third weigh fourteen. The first and third weigh twelve. How heavy is each box? Pause and try adding all three readings. Add the three readings: ten plus fourteen plus twelve is thirty-six. Look at the table. Each box was on the scales exactly twice. So thirty-six is twice the total weight, and the three boxes weigh eighteen kilograms altogether. Now subtract. The second and third weigh fourteen, so the first weighs eighteen minus fourteen, which is four. In the same way the second weighs six and the third weighs eight. Check every reading. Four and six make ten. Six and eight make fourteen. Four and eight make twelve. Watch for unequal counting. In a triangle puzzle where each side has a total, the corner numbers lie on two sides, but the middle numbers lie on only one. Adding the three side totals counts corners twice and middles once. You must keep track of that difference, not ignore it. Add the measurements. Count how often each unknown appears. Then subtract to separate them. Notebook challenge: three numbers are added in pairs to give seventeen, twenty and twenty-three. What are the three numbers?

items.title: Turn contribution limits into a sharp bound
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: If every group uses up some of a limited supply, the supply limits how many groups you can have. Twelve tokens, three per group, means at most four groups. You know that before making a single group. This gives the first half of a "largest possible" answer: a ceiling. The second half is showing that the ceiling can actually be reached. A complete solution needs both. Five students are in a club. Each day, two pairs work together and one student rests. No two students may be partners more than once. What is the largest number of days this can continue? Pause and decide what is being used up. The supply is pairs of students. Five students form ten different pairs. Each day uses two new pairs. So there can be at most five days. Can five days really be done? Here is a schedule. Day one: A with B, C with D. Day two: A with C, B with E. Day three: A with D, C with E. Day four: A with E, B with D. Day five: B with C, D with E. All ten pairs appear exactly once. What if each group has three people? Counting pairs gives a ceiling of three groups. But any two legal groups must share exactly one person. Two triples cannot be disjoint among five people, and sharing two would repeat a pair. For a third group, using the shared person repeats a pair with any other person. Leaving that person out forces three choices from the two outer pairs, so one pair repeats. Two groups fit, and a third never does. Find the limited supply. Divide to get a ceiling. Then either build an example that reaches it, or explain why it cannot be reached. Notebook challenge: six students play chess, one game per pair at most. Each day three games are played. What is the largest possible number of days?

items.title: Count the same structure from two directions
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: Four square tiles, each with side one, are pushed together to make a two by two square. What is the perimeter of the large square? We will find it by counting tile edges. Separately, each tile has four edges. Four tiles report sixteen edges altogether. When the tiles are joined, some edges end up inside. There are four inside joins: two along the vertical middle line and two along the horizontal middle line. Each inside join was reported by both tiles beside it. So remove two reports for each of the four joins. Sixteen minus eight is eight. The perimeter is eight. Check directly: the big square has side two, and four times two is eight. Now rearrange the tiles in a single row. There are only three joins, so the perimeter is sixteen minus six, which is ten. Fewer joins means a longer perimeter. The outside perimeter is the total of all tile edges, minus two for every join. Rebuild this argument, then find the perimeter of six unit squares arranged in a two by three rectangle.

items.title: Find a resource that every arrangement uses
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: When a question asks for the largest possible number, trying examples is not enough. You need a reason why nobody could ever do better. That reason usually comes from something limited that every arrangement has to use. Finding a good arrangement shows what is possible. It does not show that it is the best. Without a proof of the limit, there is always the worry that a cleverer arrangement exists. Counters are placed in a row of eight cells, at most one per cell. No two counters may be in neighbouring cells. What is the largest number of counters that can be placed? Pause and try to find both an arrangement and a reason. Split the row into four pairs of neighbouring cells. Each pair can hold at most one counter, because two counters in a pair would be neighbours. Four pairs means at most four counters. That is the limit. Now reach the limit. Put counters in cells one, three, five and seven. No two are neighbours. So four is possible, and more than four is impossible. The largest number is four. With nine cells, there are four pairs and one cell left over. Each pair holds at most one counter and the extra cell holds at most one: at most five. And cells one, three, five, seven and nine achieve it. For a smallest-number question, turn the idea around: ask what every arrangement must cover. If every empty cell must be next to a counter, each counter can look after at most three cells, itself and its two neighbours. Eight cells need at least three counters. Cells two, five and eight give that coverage, so three is enough. Find what is limited. Use it to prove a limit. Then show an arrangement that reaches the limit. Notebook challenge: what is the largest number of counters in a row of eleven cells with no two neighbours?

items.title: Explain why a promising choice is best
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: Take a fixed length of fence and make a rectangle. A long thin rectangle encloses very little. As the sides become more equal, the area grows. Balanced parts give bigger products. You could discover this by trying examples. But in a competition you need to know it is always true, and what to do when perfect balance is not allowed. Two positive whole numbers add to twelve. What is the largest their product can be? Pause and try a few pairs. One and eleven give eleven. Two and ten give twenty. Three and nine, twenty-seven. Four and eight, thirty-two. Five and seven, thirty-five. Six and six give thirty-six. The product climbs as the numbers get closer. Here is why. Write the two numbers as six minus d and six plus d. Start with a six by six square. Move a strip from one side to the other. The pieces no longer fit: a small square of side d is missing. So the product is thirty-six minus d squared. The further from balance, the more you lose. Now add a restriction: the two numbers must be different. Six and six is no longer allowed. Choose the most balanced pair that is allowed, five and seven, giving thirty-five. The number of parts matters too. Three fours give a product of sixty-four. Four threes give eighty-one. Both splits are balanced within their own number of parts, but the second product is bigger. Check how many parts the question actually allows. For two positive parts with a fixed total, the most balanced pair gives the largest product. When a rule forbids perfect balance, get as close as the rule allows. Notebook challenge: a rectangle with whole-number sides has perimeter twenty-two. What is its largest possible area?

items.title: Make equality conditions guide the construction
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: A proof of a limit is also a set of instructions. To reach the limit exactly, nothing in the proof may be wasted. Looking at where the proof is tight tells you how the best arrangement must be built. Searching for the best arrangement by trial can take a long time. Letting the proof guide you is faster, and it shows whether the limit can be reached at all. Counters are placed on a four by four board, at most one per square. Each row may contain at most two counters, and each column at most two. What is the largest number of counters? Pause and find the limit first. There are four rows, and each holds at most two counters. So there are at most eight counters. That is the limit. To reach eight, every row must be completely full, with exactly two counters. And the counters must be spread so that no column gets more than two. Putting them all in the first two columns would break the column rule. So share the columns. Rows one and two use columns one and two. Rows three and four use columns three and four. Every row has two, and every column has two. Eight is reached. Always check the finished arrangement against every rule, not only the total. An arrangement can have the right number and still break a rule somewhere. Here every row, every column and every square passes. Prove the limit. Ask what must be full to reach it. Build the arrangement, then check every rule. Notebook challenge: on a three by three board with at most one counter per row and per column, what is the largest number of counters, and where could they go?

items.title: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: Pack seven red counters and four blue counters into trays. A tray holds at most four counters, and at most two of them may be red. What is the smallest number of trays needed? There are eleven counters. Each tray holds at most four, so two trays are not enough. At least three trays are needed. But that is only a first limit. Now look at the red counters alone. Each tray takes at most two reds. Three trays could hold only six reds, and there are seven. So at least four trays are needed. This limit is stronger. Can four trays work? Fill them like this: two reds and two blues; two reds and one blue; two reds and one blue; and one red. All eleven counters are packed and every rule is obeyed. So four trays are enough, and three are not. The answer is four. Notice that some spaces are left empty. That is fine: the red rule, not the total space, decided the answer. Check each rule for a lower bound. Take the strongest bound, then build a packing that reaches it. Try it with nine red counters and three blue counters.

items.title: Build an honest sample space
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: A probability compares favourable outcomes with all outcomes, but only if the outcomes are equally likely. A bag holds two red counters and one blue. There are two colours, but red is not a one in two chance. There are three counters, each equally likely, and two of them are red. Counting names instead of real outcomes is the most common probability mistake. The fix is to list outcomes that genuinely are equally likely, then count. Toss two fair coins separately, so one result cannot affect the other. What is the probability of getting exactly one head? Someone says there are three results, two heads, one head or no heads, so the answer is one third. Pause and decide whether that is right. Give the coins names: first coin and second coin. Now there are four outcomes: head head, head tail, tail head, and tail tail. These four are equally likely. Exactly one head happens in two of the four: head tail, and tail head. So the probability is two out of four, which is one half, not one third. The three results in the earlier list were not equally likely. Roll two fair dice separately. There are thirty-six equally likely pairs. A total of seven comes from six of them, so its probability is six out of thirty-six, one sixth. A total of two comes from only one pair. The totals are not equally likely, but the pairs are. Label the objects so each outcome is visible. Check the outcomes are equally likely. Then count favourable out of total. Notebook challenge: two dice are rolled. What is the probability that the two numbers are the same?

items.title: Track how one choice changes the next
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: When you take something out and do not put it back, the situation changes. The second draw is from a different bag. To keep track, follow each possible route step by step. Using the original bag for both draws is a common error. Updating after each step is what makes the answer right. A bag holds two red counters and two blue counters. Draw two counters at random, one after the other, without putting the first back. What is the probability that both are red? Pause and think about the bag after the first draw. On the first draw, two of the four counters are red. The chance of red is two out of four, which is one half. If the first was red, the bag now has one red and two blue. The chance of red again is one out of three. Along one route, multiply: one half times one third is one sixth. So the probability of two reds is one sixth. Complete the tree. Red then blue is one half times two thirds, one third. Blue then red is also one third. Blue then blue is one sixth. The four routes add to one, which is a good check. What is the chance of one of each colour? That happens on two different routes: red then blue, or blue then red. Different routes are added: one third plus one third is two thirds. Update the situation after each step. Multiply along a route. Add separate routes. Notebook challenge: a bag has three red counters and one blue. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?

items.title: Recount within the information you are given
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: New information changes a probability. When you are told something about the result, cross out every outcome that no longer fits. What is left is your new, smaller world, and you count inside it. The usual mistake is to keep the old total on the bottom of the fraction. After information arrives, the total is the number of outcomes that survive. A fair die is rolled. You are told the result is even. What is the probability that it is greater than three? Pause and cross out what cannot have happened. The die shows one to six. "Even" removes one, three and five. Three outcomes survive: two, four and six. They are still equally likely. Of those three, the numbers greater than three are four and six. So the probability is two out of three. Without the information it would have been three out of six, one half. The information changed the answer. Roll two fair dice separately. You are told the total is eight. Five pairs survive: two and six, three and five, four and four, five and three, six and two. What is the chance that both dice show the same number? Only four and four works: one out of five. Crossing out works because outcomes that were equally likely before the information are still equally likely afterwards. If the outcomes are not equally likely, you compare their probabilities rather than just counting them. Cross out what the information rules out. Then count favourable outcomes among the survivors. Notebook challenge: a die is rolled and you are told the number is greater than two. What is the probability that it is odd?

items.title: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: Two fair coins are tossed independently. You know that at least one of them shows heads. What is the probability that both show heads? Name the coins first and second. There are four equally likely outcomes: head head, head tail, tail head, tail tail. "At least one head" rules out tail tail. Three outcomes survive: head head, head tail and tail head. They are still equally likely. Only one of the three survivors has two heads. The probability is one out of three. Compare a slightly different piece of information. Suppose you are told the first coin shows heads. Now only head head and head tail survive, and the probability of two heads is one half. The exact wording of the information matters. Information removes outcomes, and the survivors become the new total. Rebuild this example, then try: two coins are tossed and you are told they do not show the same face. What is the probability the first coin is heads?

items.title: Keep the whole visible
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: A fraction always means a fraction of something. Half of a whole bar is six squares. Half of what is left is only three squares. Same fraction, different whole, different amount. Before using any fraction, say what it is a fraction of. This matters most when things change in stages. A second fraction or percentage usually applies to the new amount, not the original. Forgetting that is the classic trap. A jar holds forty marbles. Ali takes one quarter of them. Then Bea takes one third of what remains. How many marbles are left? Pause and name the whole for each fraction. Ali's quarter is a quarter of forty, which is ten. Thirty marbles remain. Bea's third is a third of thirty, not of forty. That is ten more. Twenty marbles are left. A third of the original forty would split a marble, a clue that we have used the wrong whole. A grid shows a fraction of a fraction. Shade three of four columns: three quarters. Then take two of the three rows of that part: two thirds of three quarters. The overlap is six cells out of twelve, which is one half. To find a fraction of a fraction, multiply. Now the price trap. A one hundred dollar item goes up by ten percent, to one hundred and ten. Then it goes down by ten percent. Ten percent of one hundred and ten is eleven, so the price becomes ninety-nine. The two changes do not cancel, because they are percentages of different wholes. Always ask: fraction of what? Update the whole after each step. Notebook challenge: a tank is full. One fifth is used on Monday, and one quarter of the remainder on Tuesday. What fraction of the tank is left?

items.title: Read decimal places as divisibility conditions
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: A decimal that stops is just a fraction whose bottom number is ten, a hundred, a thousand, and so on. Nought point three seven five is three hundred and seventy-five thousandths. And every power of ten is built from twos and fives only. That one fact tells you which fractions make decimals that stop, and which go on forever, without doing any long division. Does three fortieths give a decimal that stops? And what is it? Pause and factorise forty. Forty is two times two times two times five. To make a power of ten, every two needs a five. There are three twos and one five, so supply two more fives. Multiply top and bottom by twenty-five. Three fortieths becomes seventy-five thousandths: nought point nought seven five. Now try one sixth. Six is two times three. No amount of multiplying by twos and fives can turn that three into part of a power of ten. So one sixth never stops: nought point one six six six, forever. One warning: simplify first. Six fifteenths has a three in the bottom, but it cancels. Six fifteenths is two fifths, which is nought point four. Only the simplified fraction tells the truth. Decimals also hide divisibility. Nought point two five is a quarter, so multiplying by four gives a whole number. A decimal with two places always becomes whole when multiplied by one hundred, and sometimes by something smaller. Simplify the fraction. If the bottom is built only from twos and fives, the decimal stops. If any other prime remains, it repeats forever. Notebook challenge: which of these stop: seven twentieths, five twelfths, nine seventy-fifths?

items.title: Transform equations without losing conditions
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: An equation is a balance. Take three from both sides and it stays level. Addition takes us back to the original. Halve both sides and it still balances. Doubling takes us back. A move you can undo keeps exactly the same solutions. Guessing may find an answer. Reversible moves let you solve the equation step by step and confirm you have kept all of its possible answers. Two pouches and five counters balance one pouch and twelve counters. Every pouch holds the same number. How many counters are in a pouch? Pause and think about what you could remove from both sides. Remove one pouch from each side. The balance holds. Now one pouch and five counters balance twelve counters. Remove five counters from each side. One pouch balances seven counters. Each pouch holds seven. Check in the original. Two sevens and five make nineteen. One seven and twelve make nineteen. Both sides agree. With fractions, clear them by multiplying both sides. Half a number plus three is eleven. Take three from both sides: half the number is eight. Double both sides: the number is sixteen. One caution. Before dividing by an unknown number, check whether it could be zero. If a number times itself equals five times the number and the number is not zero, dividing gives five. Zero also works, because zero times zero equals five times zero. Those two cases cover all possibilities. Do the same to both sides. Undo one operation at a time. Check your answer in the original equation. Notebook challenge: three pouches and four counters balance one pouch and eighteen counters. How many counters are in each pouch?

items.title: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: Three identical trays each hold one pouch and two loose counters. Every pouch holds the same number of counters. Altogether the trays contain twenty-one counters. How many counters are in each pouch? The three trays are identical, so they share the twenty-one counters equally. Twenty-one divided by three is seven. Each tray holds seven counters. In one tray, two of the seven counters are loose. The rest are in the pouch. Seven minus two is five. Each pouch holds five counters. In symbols: three lots of a pouch plus two equals twenty-one. So a pouch plus two equals seven, and a pouch equals five. The bars and the equation tell the same story. There is a second route. Take away all six loose counters first. Fifteen counters remain, shared by three pouches: five each. Two different orders, the same answer, which is a good check. You can share first, or remove the extras first. Rebuild both routes, then try this: four identical bags each hold one box and three loose marbles, making forty marbles altogether. How many marbles are in each box?

items.title: Build a recurrence from a reversible step
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: Some counting problems are too big to list, but they grow in a regular way. If you can explain how each case is built from smaller ones, you can climb to any size. That building rule is called a recurrence. A strip of ten cells can be tiled in eighty-nine ways. Nobody wants to list those. A recurrence gets the answer with nine small additions. A strip is covered using tiles of length one and tiles of length two. A strip of length one can be tiled in one way, length two in two ways, length three in three ways, length four in five ways. How many ways are there for length five? Pause and look at how a tiling ends. Look at the last tile. Either it is a single, and the rest is a tiling of length four. Or it is a double, and the rest is a tiling of length three. Every tiling ends in exactly one of these two ways. So the number for length five is the number for length four plus the number for length three. Five plus three is eight. Keep going. Eight plus five is thirteen. Then twenty-one, thirty-four, fifty-five, eighty-nine. Each number is the sum of the two before it. The same rule appears in disguise. Climbing stairs one or two steps at a time is the same problem: the last move is a single step or a double. Six stairs can be climbed in thirteen ways. Sort the possibilities by their last move. Each group matches a smaller case. Add the groups. Notebook challenge: how many ways are there to tile a strip of length seven with singles and doubles?

items.title: Remember enough information, but no more
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: In a process with a fixed rule, the state is everything you need to work out the next step. The same state must lead to the same next state. So once a state repeats, the whole path repeats from there. Finding the state is the key to long-run questions. Questions about the hundredth or thousandth step look impossible. But if the states repeat in a short cycle, you only need the position inside the cycle. Start with three. Each time, double the number and keep only its last digit. The list begins three, six, two, four, eight, six. What is the fiftieth number? Pause and look for a repeat. After the first number, the list repeats six, two, four, eight. Notice that three itself never comes back. The cycle starts at the second number, not the first. From the second number to the fiftieth there are forty-nine numbers. Forty-nine is twelve complete cycles and one more. So the fiftieth number is the first in the cycle: six. Sometimes one number is not enough to be the state. If each number is the last digit of the sum of the previous two, then seeing a one does not tell you what comes next. You need the last two numbers. The state is a pair. In the same way, if a robot may not reverse its last move, its position alone is not the state. You must also remember which way it just moved. Remember enough to know what can happen next, and no more. Decide what the state is. Find where a state first repeats. Then use a remainder to locate the position in the cycle. Notebook challenge: start with seven as the first number. To get each next number, triple the current one and keep only the last digit. What is the thirtieth number?

items.title: Classify game positions by their legal moves
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: In many two-player games, you can work out who should win before the game starts. Label each position as winning or losing for the player about to move, beginning with the smallest positions and working up. Playing out every possible game is hopeless. Labelling positions needs only a little work for each one, and it tells you the best move as well as the winner. Two players take turns removing one or two counters from a pile of ten. Whoever takes the last counter wins. Would you rather go first or second? Pause and think about very small piles. With one or two counters, you take them all and win. Those are winning positions. With three, whatever you take, you leave one or two, and your opponent wins. Three is a losing position. The rule is: a position is winning if some move leads to a losing position, and losing if every move leads to a winning position. From four or five you can move to three, so they are winning. Six is losing. The losing positions are the multiples of three: three, six and nine. Ten is not a multiple of three, so go first and take one, leaving nine. After that, whatever your opponent takes, you take the amount that makes three altogether. You always leave a multiple of three, and you take the last counter. Change the rule to taking one, two or three. One, two and three are winning, since you can take them all. Four is losing. From a multiple of four, any move lets the next player finish a total removal of four. From any other size, take enough to reach a multiple of four. The losing positions are the multiples of four. A position is winning if you can move to a losing one. It is losing if every move goes to a winning one. Start labelling from the end. Notebook challenge: with the take one or two rule and a pile of fourteen, what should the first player take?

items.title: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: A square of dots grows from three rows of three to four rows of four. How many dots are added? And what is the rule for growing any square to the next one? Keep the nine original dots. Add a new bottom row. The new row belongs to the bigger square, so it has four dots. Now add the new right-hand column. Its bottom dot is already there, as part of the new row. So only three more dots are needed. Four plus three is seven dots added. Nine plus seven is sixteen, which is four times four. The same picture works for any size. To grow a square of side n, add a row of n plus one dots and a column of n dots. That is two n plus one dots. So from ten by ten to eleven by eleven you add twenty-one dots. That is why the gaps between square numbers are the odd numbers: three, five, seven, nine. Rebuild this argument, then answer: how many dots are added when a twenty by twenty square grows to twenty-one by twenty-one?

items.title: Translate position into value
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: The digit four in forty-two is worth forty, because of where it stands. Swap the digits and the same four is worth only four. A digit's position multiplies its value, and writing that down turns digit puzzles into simple algebra. Digit puzzles look like guessing games. But if you write a two-digit number as ten times its first digit plus its second, most of the guessing disappears. A two-digit number is reversed, and the new number is twenty-seven bigger. What can you say about its digits? Pause and write both numbers using place value. Call the tens digit A and the units digit B. The number is ten A plus B. The reverse is ten B plus A. Subtract. The difference is nine B minus nine A, which is nine times the gap between the digits. Twenty-seven is nine times three. So the units digit is three more than the tens digit. That gives fourteen, twenty-five, thirty-six, forty-seven, fifty-eight and sixty-nine. Check one: fifty-two minus twenty-five is twenty-seven. Adding a number to its reverse gives eleven A plus eleven B: eleven times the digit sum. Forty-seven plus seventy-four is one hundred and twenty-one, which is eleven times eleven. Remember that a digit is not just any number. The first digit runs from one to nine, and the others from zero to nine. Those limits often finish a puzzle. Write numbers using place value. Reversing and subtracting gives a multiple of nine. Reversing and adding gives a multiple of eleven. Notebook challenge: a two-digit number is four times the sum of its digits. Find all such numbers.

items.title: Use information that survives rearrangement
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: Ten is one more than nine. A hundred is one more than ninety-nine. A thousand is one more than nine hundred and ninety-nine. Every place value is one more than a multiple of nine. That is why digit sums work. This gives a test for multiples of nine, and of three, that takes seconds, even for enormous numbers. It also survives when digits are rearranged. Is four thousand seven hundred and twenty-five a multiple of nine? Pause and add its digits. Each thousand leaves one over after removing nines. So four thousands leave four. Seven hundreds leave seven. Two tens leave two. The five units stay. What is left over is exactly the digit sum. Four plus seven plus two plus five is eighteen. Eighteen is a multiple of nine, so the number is too. In general, a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder when divided by nine. The digit sum lets us find the remainder, too. Five hundred and eighty-three has digit sum sixteen. Remove as many complete groups of nine from sixteen as you can. Sixteen is seven more than nine. So five hundred and eighty-three leaves remainder seven when divided by nine. Rearranging digits does not change their sum. So every arrangement of the digits one, two and six is a multiple of nine. And since nine is a multiple of three, the same digit-sum test works for three. It solves missing digits too. Five, blank, eight is a multiple of nine. The known digits add to thirteen, so the blank must be five, making eighteen. A number and its digit sum have the same remainder on division by nine, and on division by three. Notebook challenge: what digit makes seven, three, blank, four a multiple of nine?

items.title: Organise counts, inventories and next-number
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: "How many numbers contain a two?" and "How many twos are written?" are different questions. Twenty-two is one number, but it contains two twos. Decide which you are counting, then count one place at a time. Counting straight through a long list is slow and error-prone. Counting each place separately is quick, and repeated digits take care of themselves. All the whole numbers from one to one hundred are written out. How many times is the digit seven written? Pause and think about the units place first. In the units place, seven appears once in every ten numbers: seven, seventeen, twenty-seven, up to ninety-seven. That is ten times. In the tens place, seven appears in seventy to seventy-nine: ten times. Altogether the digit seven is written twenty times. Seventy-seven was counted once in each place, which is correct, because it has two sevens. Now the other question: how many numbers contain a seven? The column has ten numbers and the row has ten, but seventy-seven is in both. Ten plus ten minus one is nineteen. A related skill is counting all the digits. Numbering pages one to ninety-nine uses nine digits for the single-digit pages, and two digits each for the ninety pages from ten to ninety-nine. That is nine plus one hundred and eighty: one hundred and eighty-nine digits. Decide whether you are counting numbers or occurrences. Count each place separately. For numbers, remove any overlap. Notebook challenge: how many times is the digit three written in the numbers from one to fifty?

items.title: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: Add fifty-eight and sixty-seven, and explain what each carry really means. In the units column, eight plus seven is fifteen units. Ten of those units make one ten. Carry that ten to the next column, and five units remain. In the tens column there are five tens, six tens, and the carried ten: twelve tens. Ten of those tens make one hundred. Carry it, and two tens remain. The answer is one hundred, two tens and five units: one hundred and twenty-five. Neither starting number has a hundreds digit. The hundreds digit in the answer exists only because of the second carry. Check two ways. Roughly, sixty plus seventy is one hundred and thirty, which is close. Exactly, fifty plus sixty is one hundred and ten, eight plus seven is fifteen, and together they make one hundred and twenty-five. A carry is ten of one place traded for one of the next place. Rebuild this explanation, then add seventy-six and eighty-nine, saying what each carry means.
